threat_it_covers: secret not held as a plaintext file on disk
what_it_does_not_cover: any process sharing the same Python interpreter binary can read another program's keyring secret without an OS prompt (ACL is keyed to the interpreter, not the script)

storage_option: Python keyring (Linux Secret Service / KDE KWallet / Windows Credential Locker)
threat_it_covers: uses OS-native secret storage rather than a flat file
what_it_does_not_cover: library states "no analysis has been performed" on these backends' security properties -- no vendor-asserted threat model

storage_option: msal-extensions token cache (Windows DPAPI / macOS Keychain)
threat_it_covers: token cache encrypted at rest using the OS's own key-protection primitive
what_it_does_not_cover: none in the working case; documented for public desktop clients only, explicitly cautioned against for web apps

threat_it_covers: nothing if the caller opted into the plaintext fallback (fallback_to_plaintext=True); the README sample's default re-raises instead
what_it_does_not_cover: opt-in unencrypted fallback logs a warning; keep it off and check persistence.is_encrypted

threat_it_covers: centralizes one secret/key behind Entra-authenticated, RBAC- or access-policy-scoped access instead of replicating it to every workstation; HSM-backed at Premium tier (FIPS 140-3 L3)
what_it_does_not_cover: still requires the caller (user or application) to authenticate through Microsoft Entra ID before any access -- not a bootstrap-free mechanism

threat_it_covers: centralizes secret management and audits all access; dynamic DB credentials give each service its own leased credential instead of a password hardcoded in the service
what_it_does_not_cover: clients must first authenticate to Vault (a token, LDAP, a cloud provider such as Azure or AWS, etc.) to get an access token -- the storage problem is pushed one layer, not eliminated

threat_it_covers: bounds a machine credential's lifetime (TTL) and use count instead of an unbounded static secret
what_it_does_not_cover: SecretID itself must still be delivered once (pull vs push mode) -- an initial delivery channel is still needed

threat_it_covers: restricts a variable to protected branches/tags; masking hides the literal value in job log text
what_it_does_not_cover: masking is explicitly "not a guaranteed way to prevent" leakage -- a job can still print or exfiltrate the value deliberately or accidentally

storage_option: GitLab native secrets integration (`ci/secrets/`: Vault, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, AWS Secrets Manager) via id_tokens
threat_it_covers: secret is fetched at job run time on demand rather than pre-loaded into every job's environment like a CI/CD variable
what_it_does_not_cover: still relies on the external provider's own access control; GitLab's own docs do not enumerate this as strictly safer, only architecturally different (on-demand vs always-present)

threat_it_covers: short-lived, per-job, project-scoped credential -- nothing to store between jobs
what_it_does_not_cover: only useful for GitLab-internal API calls (registry, other GitLab projects) within the configured allowlist, not a general external-secret substitute

threat_it_covers: lets a dynamic/rotating credential (e.g. a Vault-fetched short-lived token) reach the CLI as a shell script's output instead of a static API-key env var; re-run after five minutes by default; hot-reloads on settings-file change without a session restart
what_it_does_not_cover: the helper script's own output still needs somewhere secure to originate from -- delegates back to one of the other rows

storage_option: Claude Code MCP OAuth token store
threat_it_covers: sign-ins stored per MCP server endpoint; pre-configured client secret kept out of the config (system keychain on macOS or a credentials file)
what_it_does_not_cover: the page does not name where the OAuth tokens themselves are stored, so their protection cannot be compared with the keyring/msal-extensions rows above

threat_it_covers: lets a secret live outside argv/env entirely, read once at process start from a path an operator controls
what_it_does_not_cover: the file's own filesystem permissions and disk encryption become the enforcement point -- a "secrets readable from a file path" design rule states the requirement, not a specific backend
